title: Quantifier
body:
A **quantifier** says how many objects in the domain satisfy a formula. Predicate logic has
two.

```
∀x Fx      universal:    every object in the domain is F
∃x Fx      existential:  at least one object in the domain is F
```

The pairing with connectives is the part to memorise, because each quantifier takes a different
one and swapping them changes the meaning completely:

```
"All cats are mammals"     ∀x (Cx → Mx)        conditional inside the universal
"Some cats are black"      ∃x (Cx ∧ Bx)        conjunction inside the existential
```

Using a conjunction with the universal, `∀x (Cx ∧ Mx)`, claims that everything in the domain is
a cat and a mammal. Using a conditional with the existential, `∃x (Cx → Bx)`, is true as soon
as anything at all fails to be a cat, since a false antecedent makes the
[[Material Conditional]] true, so it says almost nothing.

The two are related by negation, which is De Morgan's law with quantifiers:

```
¬∀x Fx   ≡   ∃x ¬Fx        not everything is F means something is not F
¬∃x Fx   ≡   ∀x ¬Fx        nothing is F means everything is not F
```

Order matters when quantifiers are nested. `∀x ∃y Lxy` says everybody loves somebody, possibly
a different person each time, and `∃y ∀x Lxy` says one particular person is loved by everybody.
The second entails the first and the first does not entail the second.

Derivations add an introduction and an elimination rule for each quantifier, and universal
introduction carries a side condition preventing a proof about one arbitrary object from being
generalised when that object was chosen with any special property in mind.
